This tutorial follows a daily flowering survey through data preparation,
onset-directed network construction, site comparisons, and a duration-preserving
reference model. The survey functions reuse ecoTemporalNet's interval overlap,
graph construction, degree, and persistence functions.

The data are synthetic. Presence refers to the selected phenological stage
(here, flowering), not to whether the organism exists at the site. Graph edges
represent temporal co-occurrence opportunity, not measured ecological interactions.

## Load the package

After adding the new functions to ecoTemporalNet and installing it:


``` r
library(ecoTemporalNet)
```

## Prepare survey records

Use one row per species, date, and site. The `presence` column distinguishes:

- `1`: the species was observed flowering.
- `0`: the species was surveyed and observed not flowering.
- `NA` or an omitted species/date row: flowering status is unknown.

A missing record must not be turned into zero unless the survey design actually
establishes absence. If surveys include multiple individuals, aggregate them to
a species-level status using an explicit rule before this workflow. Filter to
one phenological stage at a time.

Create complete daily observations for three species at two sites:


``` r
observations <- expand.grid(
  species = c("A", "B", "C"),
  date = as.Date("2026-04-01") + 0:9,
  site = c("north", "south"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
day <- as.integer(observations$date - as.Date("2026-04-01")) + 1L
observations$presence <- as.integer(
  (observations$species == "A" & day <= 4L) |
  (observations$species == "B" & day >= 3L & day <= 7L) |
  (observations$species == "C" & day >= 8L)
)

# Move species A later at the southern site, preserving its four-day duration.
idx <- observations$site == "south" & observations$species == "A"
observations$presence[idx] <- as.integer(day[idx] >= 6L & day[idx] <= 9L)

head(observations)
#>   species       date  site presence
#> 1       A 2026-04-01 north        1
#> 2       B 2026-04-01 north        0
#> 3       C 2026-04-01 north        0
#> 4       A 2026-04-02 north        1
#> 5       B 2026-04-02 north        0
#> 6       C 2026-04-02 north        0
```

The northern site has A flowering on days 1–4, B on days 3–7, and C on days
8–10. The southern site shifts A to days 6–9. This produces different overlap
patterns without changing species A's flowering duration.

## Build onset-directed networks


``` r
analysis <- prepare_phenology(observations)
```

The function separates records by site and calendar year. Without an explicit
`observation_window`, each group uses its first and last survey dates. The
`observed` method is the default: unknown days stay unknown, and only confirmed
shared presence contributes to edges. No days between surveys are filled.

Edges point from earlier to later first presence. Equal onsets use earlier last
presence, then species name. That rule is deterministic; it does not establish
biological precedence between species with tied onsets. When flowering has
multiple episodes, direction uses the species' first and last presence across
the whole window, while overlap counts only confirmed positive episodes.

All recorded species remain as graph vertices, including isolates. Here species
C is isolated in the northern network because it starts after B ends.


``` r
analysis$settings
#> $method
#> [1] "observed"
#> 
#> $observation_window
#> NULL
#> 
#> $direction
#> [1] "onset"
#> 
#> $directed
#> [1] TRUE
#> 
#> $onset_ties
#> [1] "earlier last presence, then species name"
#> 
#> $weight
#> [1] "overlap_days"
#> 
#> $missing
#> [1] "unknown; interval mode reconstructs species with positive records"
analysis$groups[[1]]$metadata
#>    site year start_date   end_date
#> 1 north 2026 2026-04-01 2026-04-10
igraph::as_data_frame(analysis$groups[[1]]$graph)
#>   from to weight overlap_days jointly_known_days overlap_jaccard
#> 1    A  B      2            2                 10       0.2857143
```

Group metadata identifies the site/year. The northern graph has A → B with two
shared days. Species C remains a vertex even though it is absent from the edge
table. `weight` and `overlap_days` both count shared days; `jointly_known_days`
records observation support, and `overlap_jaccard` uses jointly known days only.

Each group also stores `observations`, `observed_presence`, analysis `presence`,
calendar `dates`, positive `intervals`, and `summary`. The original input and
preparation settings are retained at the top level.

## Compare community and species summaries


``` r
community <- summarise_phenology_networks(analysis)
community[c("site", "year", "n_species", "window_days", "n_edges",
            "mean_degree", "mean_overlap_days", "days_with_presence",
            "known_empty_days", "unresolved_days")]
#>    site year n_species window_days n_edges mean_degree mean_overlap_days
#> 1 north 2026         3          10       1   0.6666667                 2
#> 2 south 2026         3          10       2   1.3333333                 2
#>   days_with_presence known_empty_days unresolved_days
#> 1                 10                0               0
#> 2                  8                2               0
```

The north has one edge and ten days with at least one species flowering. The
south has two edges but only eight flowering days: more overlap does not
necessarily mean better seasonal coverage. Species richness and study window
are equal here, but they need checking in real comparisons.


``` r
species <- summarise_phenology_networks(analysis, level = "species")
species[c("site", "species", "degree", "in_degree", "out_degree",
          "presence_days", "unknown_days", "exclusive_presence_days")]
#>    site species degree in_degree out_degree presence_days unknown_days
#> 1 north       A      1         0          1             4            0
#> 2 north       B      1         1          0             5            0
#> 3 north       C      0         0          0             3            0
#> 4 south       A      2         1          1             4            0
#> 5 south       B      1         0          1             5            0
#> 6 south       C      1         1          0             3            0
#>   exclusive_presence_days
#> 1                       2
#> 2                       3
#> 3                       3
#> 4                       0
#> 5                       3
#> 6                       1
```

Degree counts partners. Incoming and outgoing degree follow onset direction.
Exclusive presence days require the focal species to be present and all other
recorded species to be known absent. These quantities describe the recorded
species pool, which may not contain every species in the community. Labelled
site/year summaries provide descriptive comparisons, not independent-replicate
assumptions or statistical tests of site differences.

## Choose an undirected representation

For symmetric coflowering questions, choose the undirected option:


``` r
symmetric <- prepare_phenology(observations, direction = "undirected")
igraph::is_directed(analysis$groups[[1]]$graph)
#> [1] TRUE
igraph::is_directed(symmetric$groups[[1]]$graph)
#> [1] FALSE
```

Presence, overlap duration, and flowering coverage are unchanged. For these
simple graphs, total degree also agrees between representations. Connectance
uses different denominators: `n * (n - 1)` directed pairs versus
`n * (n - 1) / 2` undirected pairs. Onset-directed connectance cannot exceed
0.5 because only one direction is retained for each overlapping pair. Do not
compare connectance across direction settings as if they had the same scale.

## Compare against randomized flowering schedules


``` r
reference <- test_phenological_structure(analysis, nsim = 199, seed = 42)
reference$summary[c("site", "metric", "observed", "null_mean",
                    "null_lower", "null_upper", "n_undefined",
                    "standardized_effect", "p_upper", "p_lower")]
#>    site            metric  observed null_mean null_lower null_upper n_undefined
#> 1 north       mean_degree 0.6666667 1.5142379  0.6666667        2.0           0
#> 2 north       connectance 0.1666667 0.3785595  0.1666667        0.5           0
#> 3 north mean_overlap_days 2.0000000 2.4103853  1.0000000        4.0           0
#> 4 north    coverage_lower 1.0000000 0.7487437  0.5000000        1.0           0
#> 5 south       mean_degree 1.3333333 1.4673367  0.6666667        2.0           0
#> 6 south       connectance 0.3333333 0.3668342  0.1666667        0.5           0
#> 7 south mean_overlap_days 2.0000000 2.4731993  1.5000000        4.0           0
#> 8 south    coverage_lower 0.8000000 0.7532663  0.5000000        1.0           0
#>   standardized_effect p_upper p_lower
#> 1          -1.5978777   1.000   0.220
#> 2          -1.5978777   1.000   0.220
#> 3          -0.5863698   0.805   0.440
#> 4           1.7909108   0.070   1.000
#> 5          -0.2408037   0.735   0.535
#> 6          -0.2408037   0.735   0.535
#> 7          -0.7004799   0.865   0.400
#> 8           0.3393405   0.510   0.725
```

The reference model preserves each species' flowering duration and independently
samples a feasible onset inside the group's observation window. Species with
no presence stay absent. Intervals neither wrap around nor extend beyond the
window. Each simulated graph uses the same constructor and metrics as the
observed graph; onset directions are recalculated, not held fixed.

The example uses 199 replicates to run quickly; choose a simulation count suited
to the desired precision in an actual analysis. The supplied seed reproduces
results without altering the caller's random-number state.

Reference quantiles describe the simulated distribution, not confidence intervals
for an estimated ecological effect. Standardized effects are undefined when null
variance is zero. Mean overlap is undefined in edgeless graphs; the output counts
undefined replicates and withholds tail probabilities when they occur. Reported
tails use add-one corrections and are not adjusted for multiple comparisons.

This null model does not preserve species-specific seasonal constraints,
climate, abundance, or sampling effort. Its conclusions are conditional on the
chosen window and duration estimates. It is not evidence of a particular
interaction mechanism.

## Keep missing surveys distinct from absence

Remove two survey dates without replacing them with zeros:


``` r
missing_dates <- as.Date(c("2026-04-02", "2026-04-04"))
sparse <- observations[!(observations$date %in% missing_dates), ]
sparse_analysis <- prepare_phenology(sparse)

sparse_summary <- summarise_phenology_networks(sparse_analysis)
sparse_summary[c("site", "days_with_presence", "known_empty_days",
                 "unresolved_days", "coverage_lower", "coverage_upper",
                 "unknown_fraction")]
#>    site days_with_presence known_empty_days unresolved_days coverage_lower coverage_upper
#> 1 north                  8                0               2            0.8            1.0
#> 2 south                  7                1               2            0.7            0.9
#>   unknown_fraction
#> 1              0.2
#> 2              0.2
```

The missing days remain in the calendar matrix as `NA`. Coverage's lower bound
counts confirmed flowering days. Its upper bound additionally includes unresolved
days that could contain flowering. These are bounds on what the records establish,
not statistical confidence intervals.

The reference model rejects incomplete daily histories rather than treating
unknowns as absence. Catch the expected error here so the tutorial remains runnable:


``` r
tryCatch(
  test_phenological_structure(sparse_analysis, nsim = 19, seed = 42),
  error = function(e) message(conditionMessage(e))
)
#> Null comparisons require complete daily histories; unknown days remain.
```

## Make interval reconstruction explicit

When continuous flowering between first and last observed presence is justified,
request the interval method:


``` r
reconstructed <- prepare_phenology(sparse, method = "interval")
reconstructed_summary <- summarise_phenology_networks(reconstructed)
reconstructed_summary[c("site", "days_with_presence", "known_empty_days",
                         "unresolved_days", "coverage_lower", "coverage_upper",
                         "unknown_fraction")]
#>    site days_with_presence known_empty_days unresolved_days coverage_lower coverage_upper
#> 1 north                 10                0               0            1.0            1.0
#> 2 south                  8                2               0            0.8            0.8
#>   unknown_fraction
#> 1                0
#> 2                0
```

For species with a positive record, this method fills presence between the first
and last positive observations and assumes absence outside that span within the
window. Recorded absence inside the proposed span raises an error. Species
without positive records retain their original zeros and unknowns.

Reconstruction can change onset, end, and overlap relative to a complete survey.
In this example, missing April 4 hides the northern species A's true last presence,
so its reconstructed interval ends earlier than it actually did. Eliminating
`NA` therefore does not mean the original flowering history has been recovered.

The workflow preserves `observed_presence` separately, so assumptions can be
audited. Comparing observed-only and reconstructed analyses explores a continuity
assumption; it does not estimate detection error or endpoint uncertainty.

## Reuse existing ecoTemporalNet functions

The graph in each group is an ordinary igraph object. Existing functions remain
the source of degree and persistence summaries:


``` r
g <- analysis$groups[[1]]$graph
calculate_avg_temporal_network_degree(g)
#> [1] 0.6666667
calculate_node_temporal_degree(g, mode = "out")
#>   species degree
#> A       A      1
#> B       B      0
#> C       C      0
calculate_persistence_metrics(g) # Edge persistence only; node persistence is NA.
#>   avg_node_persistence avg_edge_persistence
#> 1                   NA                    2
```

Supply interval data to `calculate_persistence_metrics(g, species_data)` only
when species-level continuous intervals are justified. Its graph-only mode avoids
inferring node durations from incomplete survey spans. Other legacy metrics keep
their documented weighting, direction, and disconnected-graph behaviour.
